701.title: The second arrow
701.hook: the first arrow is pain; the second is our reaction to it (Samyutta Nikaya 36.6)
701.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the two arrows to describe how the mind adds suffering to pain, and meditators practice noticing bodily sensation directly while letting the added commentary pass.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was dukkha, the first truth: suffering, named plainly so it can be understood. Your line was stand next to it and look.

A dark kitchen, a glass of water, no lights on. A bare foot meets the leg of a chair, hard. That's the first part, and it's sharp, and it's real. Then the second part arrives, about half a second later. Who moved this chair. Why does this always happen to me. Now the toe hurts, and so does the whole night. Often, what keeps us awake is the second part. A short teaching of the Buddha has a name for each of them. It calls them arrows.
screen: `A BARE FOOT, A CHAIR LEG.` → `THEN, HALF A SECOND LATER…` → `TWO ARROWS.`

segments.voice: First, same pain, two people. In the Samyutta Nikaya there's a teaching called the Arrow. The Buddha says an untaught person and a trained disciple both feel things: pleasant, painful and neither. Pain comes to both. The difference is what happens next. Touched by pain, the text says, the untaught person sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast and becomes distraught. Second, one arrow, then another. It's like a man struck by an arrow, the Buddha says, and then by a second arrow right after it. Now he feels the pain of two. The first is the pain in the body. The second is the pain the mind adds: the sorrowing, the lamenting, the beating of the breast. Third, some second arrows look like comfort. The text adds that the untaught person, touched by pain, goes looking for sense pleasure, because he knows no other way out of pain. So a second arrow isn't always a rant. Sometimes it's the snack, the scroll, the drink, reached for so the first arrow doesn't have to be felt. Fourth, the first one still hurts. The trained disciple feels the first arrow and not the second: bodily pain, yes; the added layer, no. This isn't a promise of numbness. The toe still throbs. What drops away is the extra wound we fire into ourselves. And this isn't the poisoned arrow from the parable back in year one: a different teaching, the same honesty about pain.

segments.voice: Wait for something slightly uncomfortable to show up, an itch, a stiff shoulder, a sound, a worry, and find the first arrow: just the plain sensation. Then watch for the second, the commentary right behind it: ugh, not this, why now. Don't fight it; notice it as a second arrow, and come back to the first, which may be smaller than it seemed.
Trained disciple, the one who, struck by pain, feels only the first arrow and not the second one the mind adds. Today's word.
Your line: skip the second arrow. The first one is real; the second one is extra. That's day seven hundred one.

702.title: The thirst
702.hook: the second truth: suffering comes with craving (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
702.howItsDone: Buddhists study the second noble truth as part of the four noble truths, and in meditation practice noticing craving as it arises, without acting on it or suppressing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was trained disciple: one who feels the first arrow of pain, not the second. Your line was skip the second arrow. Today, what keeps the bow drawn.

Drink salt water and you get thirstier. The very thing you reach for to fix the thirst feeds it. Other things work a bit like that. One more episode, and the next one starts on its own. One more look at the phone. One more thing in the cart. Each one is supposed to settle it, and each leaves the wanting a little wider. After it names suffering, the Buddha's first teaching names where suffering comes from, with a word for thirst.
screen: `SALT WATER MAKES YOU THIRSTIER.` → `ONE MORE, AND ONE MORE.` → `A WORD FOR THIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Pali it's tanha, and the Pali-English Dictionary glosses it as thirst, and as craving: the same word does for a dry throat and a restless mind. Second, now here, now there. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the second noble truth says suffering arises with craving, bound up with delight and passion, seeking delight now here, now there. That's its restlessness. It doesn't settle on one thing and rest. It finishes one glass and looks for the next. Third, three thirsts. The same teaching names three kinds. A thirst for sense pleasures: tastes, sounds, touch, the good things. A thirst for being: to become something, to last, to be someone. And a thirst for not being: for something to stop, to go away, not to exist. That third one is easy to miss. Pushing away can be thirst, too. Wanting the feeling gone, the person gone, the day over, has the same dry, reaching quality as wanting more. Fourth, not every wish. Tanha doesn't mean wanting anything at all. The Buddha's own path asks for effort, and when a teaching on right effort describes the wish for wholesome states, it uses a different word, chanda. That wish isn't called thirst. The thirst is the grasping kind of wanting: the kind that can't stand still, and never quite says enough.

703.title: Only by love
703.hook: hatred never ends by hatred, only by love; this is an old law (Dhammapada 5)
703.howItsDone: Buddhists read and recite the Dhammapada's verses, and loving-kindness meditation is one practice used to soften resentment toward people who have caused harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tanha, the thirst that seeks delight now here, now there. Your line was now here, now there. Today, one thirst in particular: to get even.

He said that. In that tone. In front of everyone. Hours later the scene is still running: once in the shower, once in the car, and each time the comeback gets sharper. By now the argument has lasted far longer in one head than it did in the room. The other person has probably moved on to lunch. The Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, has this scene in its first chapter. It even gives the replay.
screen: `HE SAID THAT. IN THAT TONE.` → `REPLAYED IN THE SHOWER.` → `THE DHAMMAPADA KNOWS THIS SCENE.`

segments.voice: First, the replay. In Max Müller's old translation, verse three goes: "He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me." In those who harbor such thoughts, the verse says, hatred will never cease. Verse four turns it round: in those who don't harbor them, hatred will cease. The verses aren't about the insult. They're about the sentence we keep saying to ourselves afterward. Second, hatred doesn't end hatred. Then verse five: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love." It reads like common sense, and it's hard to live. Hitting back can look like ending it; the verse says it keeps it going. Third, the Pali says non-hatred. Müller chose the English word love. The Pali word is averena: by non-hatred, by the absence of enmity. So the verse isn't asking you to feel warm toward the person who wronged you, not today anyway. It's asking you to stop adding fuel. Love, in this verse, can start as simply putting the replay down. Fourth, an old rule. That's what the verse calls it. Not a clever tactic for winning, just how hatred works, the way fire works. Feed it, and it burns. Stop feeding it, and it goes down.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small hostility, not the deepest wound: a sharp email, a neighbor, a relative's comment. Hear its replay sentence once, the he said, she did, then let it trail off each time it starts, the way you'd stop feeding a fire. You don't need to forgive or feel warm; just don't add a log, and rest with the breath.

Your line: stop feeding it. Hatred ceases by its absence, not by more of it. See you tomorrow.

704.title: The mind leads
704.hook: all that we are is the result of what we have thought (Dhammapada 1)
704.carry: like a wheel or a shadow
704.howItsDone: Buddhists read the Dhammapada's opening pair of verses as a teaching on intention: the state of mind behind speech and action shapes what follows, and meditation is one way of watching that happen.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was averena: hatred ceases by non-hatred, not by more hatred. Your line was stop feeding it. Today, the verse that opens the whole book.

Which came first this morning, the mood or the thought? A message from a friend sits unanswered for three hours. A thought arrives: they're annoyed with me. Nobody said so. But within a minute the shoulders are up, the coffee tastes flat, and someone at home gets a short answer they didn't earn. Then the friend replies: sorry, phone died. The mood had already done its work. The Dhammapada's very first verse puts the mind at the front of that chain.
screen: `AN UNANSWERED MESSAGE.` → `A THOUGHT: THEY'RE ANNOYED.` → `THE MOOD DOES ITS WORK.`

segments.voice: First, a big English line. Max Müller's old translation of the first verse begins: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." It's a sweeping sentence. Second, the Pali is plainer. The verse opens with a few short words: states have mind as their forerunner, mind as their chief, and are made of mind. Mano pubbangama: the mind goes in front. It walks ahead, and what we say and do comes along behind it. Third, two pictures. If someone speaks or acts with an evil thought, the verse goes on, "pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage." The ox steps, and the heavy wheel rolls over the same ground. The second verse is the mirror: speak or act with a pure thought, and "happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him." One grinds along behind you; one goes wherever you go, without any weight at all. Fourth, what it's about. These verses join a state of mind, then speaking or acting from it, then what follows. They aren't saying a gloomy thought makes it rain, or that someone ill thought their way there. They're about the short road from mind to mouth to hands: they're annoyed, then tight shoulders, then a short answer at home.

segments.voice: Wait for a thought, any thought, a plan, a memory, a worry, and when it comes, don't follow it out the door. Stay put and watch what it does inside: does the chest tighten or soften, does a mood start to gather? See if you can catch the moment the thought steps in front and the mood falls in behind, then let it go and wait for the next.

705.title: Patacara's grief
705.hook: Patacara loses her whole family in a day, runs mad with grief, and later becomes a respected teacher (Therigatha commentary)
705.howItsDone: Buddhists tell Patacara's story from the commentaries and read her verses in the Therigatha, the poems of the early nuns.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was mano pubbangama: the mind goes in front. Your line was like a wheel or a shadow. Today, a story from the early nuns.

A daughter of a wealthy family in the city of Savatthi falls in love with a servant in her parents' house. Her family will never allow it, so the two slip away and make a life somewhere poor and far off. In time, a child is born. Expecting a second, she wants to go home to her mother to give birth, so with her husband and little boy she sets out for Savatthi. Her name is Patacara, and on this road she loses everything.
screen: `A RICH GIRL AND A SERVANT.` → `THE ROAD HOME TO SAVATTHI.` → `PATACARA.`

segments.voice: First, one road, one storm, one river. The story is told in the old commentary on the poems of the early Buddhist nuns. On the road a great storm breaks, and her labor begins. Her husband goes to cut branches for a shelter; a snake bites him, and he dies in the brush. She gives birth in the rain. In the morning a river is in flood. She carries the newborn across and lays him on the bank. Halfway back for her older boy, a hawk swoops down on the baby. She screams and waves her arms, and her older son, thinking she's calling him, steps into the river and is swept away. In the city she learns that in the night her parents' house fell in the storm, and her parents and brother are being burned on a single pyre. Second, come back to yourself. The story says she lost her mind. Her clothes fell from her; she wandered the streets, and people threw rubbish and drove her off. She came to the grove where the Buddha was teaching, and he said to her, in effect: sister, recover your mindfulness. And she did. Someone threw her a cloak. Third, her own poem. Patacara became a nun, and verses under her name survive in the Therigatha itself. In them she washes her feet, watches the water run down the slope, and her mind gathers, the way a good horse is trained. Fourth, a teacher. The Anguttara Nikaya names her foremost among the nuns who knew the discipline, the rules of the order. Her poem ends with a lamp, and tomorrow we'll get to it.

706.title: It can end
706.hook: the third truth: suffering can cease, what Buddhists call nibbana, a going-out like a flame
706.carry: a flame that has gone out
706.howItsDone: Buddhists study nibbana as the third noble truth, the ending of craving, and Buddhist schools describe it in different words; meditators practice letting craving cool rather than feeding or forcing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Patacara's grief: a nun who lost everything, came back to herself, and walked on. Your line was she walked on. Today, the lamp at the end of her poem.

At the end of a long dinner, somebody leans over and blows out the candle. A thin line of smoke goes up, and then nothing. Where did the flame go? Not to the kitchen, or out the window. It just isn't burning anymore. The question sounds almost silly, but in the Buddha's teaching it turns out to be a serious one. The third of his four noble truths is good news, and its word comes from a fire going out.
screen: `SOMEONE BLOWS OUT THE CANDLE.` → `WHERE DID THE FLAME GO?` → `THE THIRD TRUTH IS GOOD NEWS.`

segments.voice: First, the third truth. In the Buddha's first teaching, after naming suffering and its source, the thirst, he names this: suffering can cease. It ceases, the text says, with the fading away and ending of that very craving, letting it go, being released from it. Not a new thing added; a thirst that stops. Second, the word. In Pali it's nibbana; the Sanskrit form is nirvana. The dictionary of the old Pali texts gives its plain sense as the going out of a lamp or a fire. A related word, nibbuta, means cooled, put out. So the picture isn't a bright new place. It's a fire that has stopped burning, the heat gone out of it. Third, Patacara's lamp. At the end of her poem in the Therigatha, after watching water run down the slope, she takes a lamp into her room, sits on her bed, and draws out the wick with a needle. As the lamp goes out, her poem says, her mind was freed: the two in the same moment. Fourth, which way did the fire go? In another teaching, a wanderer named Vacchagotta keeps asking where an awakened one goes after death. The Buddha asks him back: if a fire in front of you went out, would you know it had gone out? Yes. And which way did it go, east, west, north or south? The question doesn't fit, says Vacchagotta. A fire that's gone out doesn't go anywhere. The Buddha doesn't answer with a map. He answers with a flame that has gone out.
screen: `THE THIRD TRUTH: IT CAN END.` · `NIBBANA: A FLAME GOING OUT.` · `PATACARA'S LAMP.` · `WHICH WAY DID THE FIRE GO?` · then, large: `IT CAN END.`

It may not go out; see if it cools, even a little.

707.title: Eight parts of a path
707.hook: the fourth truth: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration
707.howItsDone: Buddhists study the noble eightfold path as the fourth noble truth; in daily life practitioners often work with one factor at a time, such as right speech or right livelihood, alongside meditation for effort, mindfulness and concentration.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was nibbana, a flame going out: the third truth, that suffering can end. Today, the last of the four truths, and the end of the week.

Three truths in, a practical question shows up. Suffering has a plain name. The thirst behind it has been found. And it can end, like a lamp going out. So what happens on Wednesday morning, with the dishes, the commute and the email that needs answering? The Buddha's first teaching doesn't leave that hanging. Its fourth truth isn't another idea. It's a path of eight parts, and most of them look a lot like an ordinary day.
screen: `THREE TRUTHS IN.` → `SO WHAT HAPPENS ON WEDNESDAY?` → `THE FOURTH TRUTH IS A PATH.`

segments.voice: First, a middle way. In the Samyutta Nikaya, before he names any of the four truths, the Buddha names two roads to avoid: chasing sense pleasures, and tormenting yourself. Both, he says, are unprofitable. Between them runs a middle way, and that middle way is this path. Second, the eight parts. Right view. Right intention. Right speech. Right action. Right livelihood. Right effort. Right mindfulness. Right concentration. Notice how few of them happen on a cushion. Speech is what comes out at the checkout. Action is what the hands do. Livelihood is how the rent gets paid. Third, a nun sorts them. In the Majjhima Nikaya, a layman puts questions to the nun Dhammadinna, and one of her answers groups the eight into three. Speech, action and livelihood belong to virtue. Effort, mindfulness and concentration belong to concentration. View and intention belong to wisdom. So the path has a shape: how you live with others, how you train the mind, and how you see. Fourth, one step at a time. This week circled the first three truths: the second arrow and the thirst, hatred that ends only by love, the mind that leads, Patacara's grief and her lamp. What hurts, where it comes from, and that it can end. The fourth truth is the one you walk. And a path of eight parts is still walked one step at a time, on one ordinary day, starting with whichever step the day hands you.
screen: `A MIDDLE WAY BETWEEN TWO ROADS.` · `EIGHT PARTS, MOSTLY ORDINARY.` · `DHAMMADINNA SORTS THEM INTO THREE.` · `ONE STEP AT A TIME.` · then, large: `ONE STEP OF EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Walk through the eight slowly, one per breath: view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration. On the second time through, notice which one catches, maybe speech because of a conversation coming later, and let that one stay while the others rest. Then see where today will meet it: the room, the person, the hour.
Middle way, the Buddha's fourth noble truth: a path of eight parts, between chasing pleasure and tormenting yourself, walked one step at a time. Today's word.
Your line: one step of eight. Seven days, four truths, one path. That's a week.

chat.says: Is the Buddha's path mostly about sitting and meditating?
options: Only partly; speech, action and livelihood are on it too, so much is ordinary life.
Yes, all eight parts happen on the cushion, in long hours of sitting.

chat.meaning: The eight parts include speech, action and livelihood. Dhammadinna groups them as virtue, concentration and wisdom: how you live, train the mind, and see.
